evidence.claim: Tallgrass prairie and Osage Hills connect Pawhuska with the wider highway
evidence.quote: proceeding east along Hwy 60 through Pawhuska to Bartlesville. The byway travels through the beautiful Osage Hills

evidence.claim: The Osage Nation Heritage Trail follows Highway 60 from Ponca City through Pawhuska to Bartlesville, crossing the Osage Hills.
evidence.quote: The Osage Nation Heritage Trail is identified as beginning in Ponca City and proceeding east along Hwy 60 through Pawhuska to Bartlesville. The byway travels through the beautiful Osage Hills

evidence.claim: Oklahoma’s tourism department includes it among the state’s scenic byways and highlights tallgrass prairie and Osage Hills State Park’s rocky bluffs and forests.
evidence.quote: You’ll find expanses of Tallgrass prairie as well as Osage Hills State Park with its rocky bluffs, lush forests

evidence.claim: East of Ponca City, the highway crosses the Arkansas River, then runs 21 miles before its next state-highway junction southeast of Burbank.
evidence.quote: Upon crossing the Arkansas, US-60 enters Osage County and the Osage Nation reservation, which is coterminous with the county. US-60 does not have another junction with a state highway for 21 miles (34 km), when it comes to an intersection with SH-11 and SH-18 southeast of Burbank.

evidence.claim: The Tallgrass Prairie Preserve lies north of Pawhuska. In town, the Osage Nation Museum brings together historical photographs and objects with both traditional and contemporary Osage art.
evidence.quote: The Tallgrass Prairie Preserve lies north of the town.

evidence.claim: In town, the Osage Nation Museum brings together historical photographs and objects with both traditional and contemporary Osage art.
evidence.quote: The Osage Nation Museum (ONM) in Pawhuska, Oklahoma, is devoted to Osage history, art, and culture. Highlights include an extensive photograph collection, historical artifacts, and traditional and contemporary art.

evidence.claim: U.S. 60 reached Oklahoma through a westward extension approved in 1930.
evidence.quote: On May 29, 1930, AASHO approved an extension westward to Amarillo, Texas, bringing the route through Oklahoma for the first time.

evidence.claim: Here it replaced State Highway 11 between Ponca City and Pawhuska and State Highway 25 east toward Vinita.
evidence.quote: SH-11 (from Ponca City to Pawhuska), and SH-25 (from Pawhuska to Vinita).

evidence.claim: Later projects changed how travelers crossed the country: a 1952 rerouting bypassed Ponca City to the south and crossed a new Arkansas River bridge.
evidence.quote: The US-60 system through Ponca City was next to be reworked, on July 14, 1952. The previous US-60 and US-77 Belt Line routes and City Routes were removed in favor of a new US-60 route bypassing the city to the south on Harding Avenue and proceeding east across a new Arkansas River bridge

evidence.claim: In 1958, a straighter alignment replaced a curving section west of Pawhuska.
evidence.quote: A 3.1-mile (5.0 km) segment of US-60/SH-11 west of Pawhuska with many curves was replaced with a newer, straighter alignment on October 6, 1958

evidence.claim: Travel east from Ponca City past the Burbank junction to Pawhuska, where the Osage Nation’s government remains based.
evidence.quote: The Osage tribal government, which opened offices in Pawhuska in 1872 when its reservation was established in Indian Territory, continues to be based in Pawhuska.

evidence.claim: Travel east from Ponca City past the Burbank junction to Pawhuska, where the Osage Nation’s government remains based.
evidence.quote: From the SH-18 junction, the highways' next state highway junction lies 20 miles (32 km) further east, in Pawhuska

evidence.claim: From Pawhuska, U.S. 60 turns north, then east again toward the spur to Osage Hills State Park.
evidence.quote: North of Pawhuska, US-60 splits off to the east once again, as SH-99 continues north to the Kansas line. US-60 serves as the northern terminus of a spur route to Osage Hills State Park

evidence.claim: Beyond the park turnoff, the road enters Bartlesville and follows Adams Boulevard through downtown.
evidence.quote: US-60 turns to the east along Adams Boulevard, splitting away from SH-123, and fully enters Washington County. US-60 runs through downtown Bartlesville on Adams

evidence.claim: Burbank grew from a farming and ranching town of about 200 people into an oil-boom community of 3,000.
evidence.quote: Burbank had about 200 residents and an economy based on farming and ranching until May 1920 when E.W. Marland discovered petroleum northeast of the town.

evidence.claim: Burbank grew from a farming and ranching town of about 200 people into an oil-boom community of 3,000.
evidence.quote: Burbank quickly grew into a town of 3,000 people.

evidence.claim: E. W. Marland’s petroleum discovery northeast of town in May 1920 began that expansion.
evidence.quote: until May 1920 when E.W. Marland discovered petroleum northeast of the town.  Burbank became a boom town

evidence.claim: The Osage retained collective mineral rights and received royalties from the field, even as oil companies leased the land.
evidence.quote: The Osage tribe and its members received $45 million in royalties from the Burbank field in the 1920s.   The Osage, unlike many tribes, had retained collective ownership of mineral rights

evidence.claim: The Osage retained collective mineral rights and received royalties from the field, even as oil companies leased the land.
evidence.quote: Leases of oil land were obtained from the Osage Indians

evidence.claim: Lease auctions usually took place beneath Pawhuska’s Million Dollar Elm, where oilmen including Marland, Frank Phillips and William G. Skelly bid.
evidence.quote: Leases of oil land were obtained from the Osage Indians, usually by auction under the "Million Dollar Elm" tree in Pawhuska

evidence.claim: Lease auctions usually took place beneath Pawhuska’s Million Dollar Elm, where oilmen including Marland, Frank Phillips and William G. Skelly bid.
evidence.quote: Rich and famous oilmen such as Marland, Frank Phillips, L. E. Phillips, Waite Phillips, and William G. Skelly stood in the shade of the Elm tree and bid in the auctions.

evidence.claim: The field’s production peaked in 1923, then dropped by half in 1926.
evidence.quote: Oil production in the Burbank field expanded from 134,408 barrels in 1920 to a peak production of 26,206,741 barrels in 1923.  Production dropped by one-half in 1926

evidence.claim: By 1930 the boom was over and the population had fallen to 372.
evidence.quote: by 1930 the boom period was over.  Burbank's population dropped to 372 in 1930.

evidence.claim: The Osage Nation’s government opened offices in Pawhuska in 1872 and remains based here.
evidence.quote: The Osage tribal government, which opened offices in Pawhuska in 1872 when its reservation was established in Indian Territory, continues to be based in Pawhuska.

evidence.claim: The Osage Nation Museum, founded in 1938, holds photographs, historical objects, and traditional and contemporary art.
evidence.quote:
Highlights include an extensive photograph collection, historical artifacts, and traditional and contemporary art.
Founded in 1938

evidence.claim: Its collections include artifacts and documents donated by historian Louis F. Burns.
evidence.quote: Historian Louis F. Burns donated much of his extensive personal collection of artifacts and documents to the museum.

evidence.claim: The museum is the oldest tribally owned museum in the United States; the Nation also maintains archives and historic-preservation and cultural offices.
evidence.quote: the ONM is the oldest tribally owned museum in the United States.

evidence.claim: The museum is the oldest tribally owned museum in the United States; the Nation also maintains archives and historic-preservation and cultural offices.
evidence.quote: The Osage Nation also has a historic preservation office, archives, and cultural office.

evidence.claim: Language work continues in the city, too: the Osage Nation governs Daposka Ahnkodapi Schools, which provides Osage-language immersion.
evidence.quote: It has a program of immersion in the Osage language, and the Osage Nation tribe governs the school.

evidence.claim: The school opened in 2015, and incorporates the language into everyday routines.
evidence.quote: It opened in 2015

evidence.claim: The school opened in 2015, and incorporates the language into everyday routines.
evidence.quote: Osage language school instructions are incorporated in routines.

evidence.claim: A lone chimney, foundations and an amphitheater mark the former workers’ housing area at the north end of Osage Hills State Park.
evidence.quote: The CCC workers were housed at the north end of the park. The remnants of the housing area still visible include concrete and rock foundations, an amphitheater and a lone chimney.

evidence.claim: Civilian Conservation Corps construction began in 1935, making this one of Oklahoma’s seven original state parks.
evidence.quote: Osage Hills State Park is one of the seven original parks constructed for the State of Oklahoma by members of the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC). Construction began in 1935.

evidence.claim: Workers used locally obtained stone and timber in their buildings.
evidence.quote: The workers built structures using stone and timber that were obtained locally.

evidence.claim: Eight guest cabins remain in use, with modernized interiors but their original appearance.
evidence.quote: Eight guest cabins are still used today. Although their appearance is the same as when they were built, they have all been modernized

evidence.claim: A large picnic shelter has two stone fireplaces at opposite ends, another substantial piece of the park’s built landscape.
evidence.quote: The park also has a large picnic shelter that is suitable for use by large groups. It has a kitchen, a large dining area, and two stone fireplaces on opposite sides of the building.

evidence.claim: Outside the buildings, hiking trails cross the park, and Sand Creek runs through its southern end.
evidence.quote: Miles of hiking trails cross the park

evidence.claim: Outside the buildings, hiking trails cross the park, and Sand Creek runs through its southern end.
evidence.quote: Sand Creek at the south end of the park.
